title: MEG-XL: Data-Efficient Brain-to-Text via Long-Context Pre-Training
claim: Pre-training on much longer input context lets our model match or beat prior methods with far less labelled data.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: method schematic, context-length bar chart, accuracy bar chart
description: Three-part horizontal figure. The left panel is a two-step schematic. Step 1, pre-train with any MEG: Rest, Motor and Speech recording boxes feed cylinder datasets, which converge on a small neural network icon, with a masked-token-prediction strip beside it. Step 2, fine-tune for MEG word decoding: a person sitting in an MEG scanner feeds a network that outputs a decoded sentence with the differing words in red, and a speaker icon plays the spoken sentence. The middle panel is a bar chart of input context length. Several short blue bars for prior foundation models (0.5s to 30s) sit next to one tall red MEG-XL bar at 150s, with a '5-300x longer' arrow. The right panel is a grouped bar chart of top-10 accuracy on three datasets, with blue prior SOTA bars next to red MEG-XL bars. Red multiplier labels (2.0x, 1.5x, 1.0x) mark the gains. Blue and red contrast carries the comparison throughout.
caption: MEG-XL introduces long-context MEG pre-training. When fine-tuned, this approach generalises to decoding words in brain-to-text with less labelled subject data than required by the supervised state-of-the-art (SOTA) and brain foundation models (FMs).
abstract: Clinical brain-to-text interfaces are designed for paralysed patients who cannot provide extensive training recordings. Pre-training improves data-efficient generalisation by learning statistical priors across subjects, but these priors critically depend on context. While natural speech might unfold gradually over minutes, most methods pre-train with only a few seconds of context. Thus, we propose MEG-XL, a model pre-trained with 2.5 minutes of MEG context per sample, 5-300x longer than prior work, and equivalent to 191k tokens, capturing extended neural context. Fine-tuning on the task of word decoding from brain data, MEG-XL matches supervised performance with a fraction of the data (e.g. 1hr vs 50hrs) and outperforms brain foundation models. We find that models pre-trained with longer contexts learn representations that transfer better to word decoding. Our results indicate that long-context pre-training helps exploit extended neural context that other methods unnecessarily discard. Code, model weights, and instructions are available at https://github.com/neural-processing-lab/MEG-XL .
